cue: Red turns dark, and the picture runs slowly, then jumps ahead.

BEE.note: their green drawn as red, their blue as green; ultraviolet goes to blue

rows: Most insects see less than a sixtieth as much detail as people do.
Bees have no colour-sensing cells for red, so red flowers and objects look dark to them.
In bright light, a honeybee can see a light flicker up to 200 times a second, where people stop at about 60. This view runs slowly and then jumps ahead to suggest the difference.
Bees can see ultraviolet light, which people can’t. Phone cameras capture very little of it, so the blue in this view stands in for it.
A bee sees green, blue and ultraviolet. Since a screen can’t show ultraviolet, this view moves every colour over by one: a bee’s green appears as red, its blue as green, and its ultraviolet as blue.

spectrum.name: shift

spectrum.name: neutral
spectrum.note: where the animal sees no colour and a person does, a faint shimmer like heat haze (atlas 4)

pace.name: replay
pace.note: a tap replays the last moment three times slower

overlay.name: off
overlay.note: the view without the sky's pattern

overlay.name: polar
overlay.note: fine strokes over the sky, strongest 90 degrees from the sun, along the direction the light is polarized (atlas 6)

On this trial the colours come from the honeybee's three measured receptor classes, ultraviolet in the bluest slot. The camera's colours and the ultraviolet guess are the app's.
A tap keeps the last moment and plays it three times slower, as a faster eye might have time for it. The ratio is the app's guess.

Many insects see the direction in which sky light is polarized, strongest in a band 90 degrees from the sun, and steer by it. With &draw=polar and the motion sensors on, fine strokes show that band from the time, the date and the phone's heading. The latitude is taken as 35 degrees north, and the drawing is the app's.
